Ghostwatch is set to be revisited 34 years after millions of viewers were left terrified they were watching a real-life paranormal investigation ‘live’ on TV.

The one-off documentary takes a look back at the programme that blurred the lines between fact and fiction, exploring the story behind the notorious 1992 BBC broadcast.

Through interviews with those involved and viewers who experienced it first-hand, Ghostwatch: The Night that Terrified Britain examines the controversy, backlash and cultural impact of a programme that continues to fascinate more than three decades later.

It will also reveal exactly how the television nightmare happened — and why its reputation has endured.

What was Ghostwatch?

The original Ghostwatch programme aired to 11 million viewers on Halloween night (October 31) in 1992.

Those watching believed they were witnessing a genuine and live ghost-hunting investigation from their own front rooms. And they believed the supernatural activity was real. Children watching alongside their parents were among those also left terrified.

The ‘investigation’ took place in a family home in Northolt, north west London. It was hosted by trusted TV star Michael Parkinson, children’s presenter Sarah Greene and her husband Mike Smith. Craig Charles also played himself as a ‘roving reporter’.

Ghostwatch viewers were so spooked by the apparent live event that it sparked huge hysteria across the UK. But the trouble was, it was all fake.

The BBC had credited horror writer Stephen Volk in the opening titles. The programme also began with the Screen One drama branding.

And, later in the evening, a BBC2 announcer said: “It is of course Halloween and if you were with us for our Ghostwatch earlier, may I reassure you that it was just a story. All’s well here at Television Centre.”

However, these signals escaped frightened viewers.

In the end, the BBC received an estimated 50,000 complaints, and the fallout fuelled weeks of tabloid coverage. In 1995, the Broadcasting Standards Council criticised the BBC for failing to do more than just hint that the programme was fictional.

Ghostwatch was never repeated on the BBC again. Yet the programme went on to become a cult favourite, rather than simply disappearing into television history.

Ghostwatch: The Night that Terrified Britain revisits BBC show

Channel 5 is set to air new documentary Ghostwatch: The Night that Terrified Britain this October. It will look back on the TV hoax that has gone down in the history books and lift the lid on how it all happened.

The documentary will feature exclusive interviews with Ghostwatch’s creator Stephen and presenter Craig. There will also be television reports from the time, views from TV critics and first-and memories from those who watched it.

Damian O’Hara, senior acquisitions manager at 5 and Paramount, explains: “Ghostwatch became something of a TV legend after transmission, and its creation – and even the events of the broadcast itself – were shrouded in mystery for years.

“So to have the ability to delve back into the nostalgia of Halloween 1992 was a wonderful opportunity to bring such a unique and often unbelievable story to the 5 audience.”

Claire McArdle, from production company CMG, adds “Ghostwatch was one of the seminal TV viewing moments of my teens. A real ‘did I remember that right?!’ moment.

“So it’s been fantastic to relive every terrifying second of one of the greatest dramas in British TV history and explore the impact it has had in the decades since broadcast.”

When does Ghostwatch: The Night that Terrified Britain air?

Ghostwatch: The Night that Terrified Britain will air exactly 34 years to the days that Ghostwatch was first broadcast.

The documentary can be watched at 9.15pm on Channel 5 on Saturday October 31, 2026. It runs for one hour and 25 minutes, with an end time of 10.40pm.
